title: Hariṃ harantam: the gods follow Hari
theme: Hari, whom the gods follow, the ruler of all and chief among minds, is asked to let the Veda come whole to the speaker, to spare the path the speaker has made, and to stride forth.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «हरिं विष्णुरूपम्» — Hari, in the form of Viṣṇu
The anonymous commentator: «भक्तानां पापं हरन्तम्» — who takes away the sin of his devotees

words.role: main verb of the first line
words.context: The anonymous commentator: they follow him as servants: «भृत्यभावेनानुसरन्ति»
The anonymous commentator: «विश्वस्य जगत ईशानम्» — ruler of the world
The anonymous commentator: «श्रेष्ठत्वेन नियन्तारं» — the one who governs them by being the highest
The anonymous commentator: «मतीनां सर्वप्राणिबुद्धीनां» — of the minds of all living beings
The anonymous commentator: «ब्रह्म वेदचतुष्टयं» — the four Vedas
The anonymous commentator: «समान्यपशब्दादिवैषम्यरहितानि रूपाणि प्रकृतिप्रत्ययादीनि यस्य तत्सरूपम्» — whose forms (stems, suffixes and the rest) are even, free of faulty words
The anonymous commentator: «मा मामन्वागादन्वागच्छतु» — may it come to me
The anonymous commentator: «इदं सर्वैस्त्रैवर्णिकैः प्रत्यक्षत्वेनाधीयमानम्» — this, studied openly by all of the three varṇas (the commentator’s gloss)
The anonymous commentator: «संपादितं मोक्षमार्गं मा विवधीर्मा हिंसय» — the path to liberation we have prepared: do not destroy it
The anonymous commentator: «दातुमुद्यमं कुर्वित्यर्थः» — that is, make the effort to give

sandhi.type: ā + i → e; m and t before a vowel
sandhi.rule: mā + idam → medam (P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः)); idam āgāt joins unchanged; āgāt + ayanam → āgād ayanam (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)).

sandhi.type: visarga after ī before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: The visarga of vivadhīḥ becomes r before v.

samasa.meaning: whose forms are even, whole in form

morphology.note: Two words are written मा in this line: the first is the enclitic pronoun ‘me’ (joined with idam to medam); the second is the prohibitive particle with vivadhīḥ.
A root aorist of √gā with ā, separated from its preverb anu (tmesis); the commentator renders it as a wish (anvāgacchatu).
An aorist of the root vadh (supplying the aorist of √han), with vi, used with mā as a prohibition.

translation.literal: The gods follow Hari, who carries off, the ruler of all, the bull of thoughts. The sacred word, whole in its form, this, has come after me; do not destroy the course; stride forth.
translation.readable: The gods follow Hari, who takes away, the ruler of all, chief among minds. May this sacred word come to me whole; do not destroy the path we have made; stride forth.

anvaya: देवाः हरन्तम् विश्वस्य ईशानम् मतीनाम् वृषभम् हरिम् अनुयन्ति । इदम् सरूपम् ब्रह्म मा अनु आगात् । अयनम् मा विवधीः । विक्रमस्व ।
syntax: A statement (anuyanti) with Hari as object and three descriptions; then a statement or wish with brahma as subject and the separated verb anu … āgāt; then a prohibition (mā vivadhīḥ) and an imperative (vikramasva), both addressed to Hari.

ambiguities.note: The verse does not say what Hari carries off. The commentator: the sin of his devotees.
Literally ‘course, path’. The commentator: the path to liberation that we have prepared.
‘Stride forth’, a word often used of Viṣṇu’s strides; the commentator explains it as ‘make the effort to give’.
The commentator: the chief of the minds of all beings, who moves them to merit and demerit, and he quotes the Gāyatrī: «धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात्».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: One triṣṭubh verse printed in two lines of 22 syllables.

beginner: This verse begins with praise. The gods follow Hari, a name the old commentator explains as Viṣṇu, the one who takes away the wrongs of those devoted to him. He rules everything, and he is the chief of all minds; the commentator adds that he moves the thoughts of every being, and quotes the Gāyatrī mantra’s line about the one who inspires our thoughts. Then come three requests. May the sacred word, the Veda, come to me whole and correct. Do not destroy the path I have made. Stride forth. The commentator explains the Veda as the four Vedas, the path as the way to liberation, and the last word as a request that Hari make the effort to give.
analogy: Like a student asking a teacher that the whole lesson, not a garbled piece of it, come through to them.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the gods follow Hari, ruler of all and chief of minds; it asks that the sacred word come to the speaker, that the path not be destroyed, and that Hari stride forth.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: Hari is Viṣṇu, who takes away his devotees’ sin; the gods follow him as servants; brahma is the four Vedas, correct in every form, and the speaker asks that by his grace they come to him; ayanam is the path to liberation.

commentary.q: A gloss to report as the commentator’s
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator describes this Veda as studied openly by all of the three varṇas («सर्वैस्त्रैवर्णिकैः प्रत्यक्षत्वेनाधीयमानम्»). That is his gloss, reported as his; the verse itself says only ‘this’.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this verse is in the edition’s sources. Only the anonymous commentator comments on it, and his reading is a prayer to the Lord (paramātman) without a school argument; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this verse, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The verse asks that what is handed down arrive whole, its forms intact. Anyone who has learnt something from a teacher knows how easily a lesson can be half-heard. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What is something you learnt from someone older that you want to keep exactly as you received it?
reflect.deeper: Why might a prayer for the Veda to come to the speaker follow a verse about turning death away?
reflect.practice: Write down, as exactly as you can, one thing a teacher once told you.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it (the concordance maps are empty here, correctly).

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text begins this anuvāka with शचीभिः, the last word of 10.48, after that verse’s number (corrections.json, a witness error); the base and the Ānandāśrama text do not.
